source.module_title: Matthew Henry's Complete Commentary on the Whole Bible

sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen16149" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="31" osisID="Isa.31" sID="Isa.31"/> <div eID="gen16149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16150" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16151" type="x-p"/> This chapter is an abridgment of the foregoing chapter; the heads of it are much the same. Here is, I. A woe to those who, when the Assyrian army invaded them, trusted to the Egyptians, and not to God, for succour, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1-Isa.31.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. Assurance given of the care God would take of Jerusalem in that time of danger and distress, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4-Isa.31.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. III. A call to repentance and reformation, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.6-Isa.31.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. IV. A prediction of the fall of the Assyrian army, and the fright which the Assyrian king should thereby be put into, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8-Isa.31.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>.

(<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen16152" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because <hi type="italic">they are</hi> many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ! <hi type="super">2</hi> Yet he also <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise, and will bring evil, and will not call back his words: but will arise against the house of the evildoers, and against the help of them that work iniquity. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now the Egyptians <hi type="italic">are</hi> men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall stretch out his hand, both he that helpeth shall fall, and he that is holpen shall fall down, and they all shall fail together. <hi type="super">4</hi> For thus hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spoken unto me, Like as the lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, when a multitude of shepherds is called forth against him, <hi type="italic">he</hi> will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them: so shall the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion, and for the hill thereof. <hi type="super">5</hi> As birds flying, so will the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts defend Jerusalem; defending also he will deliver <hi type="italic">it; and</hi> passing over he will preserve it. <div eID="gen16152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16153" type="x-p"/> This is the last of four chapters together that begin with woe; and they are all woes to the sinners that were found among the professing people of God, to the <hi type="italic">drunkards of Ephraim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">ch. xxviii. 1</reference>), to <hi type="italic">Ariel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">ch. xxix. 1</reference>), to the <hi type="italic">rebellious children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.1">ch. xxx. 1</reference>), and here to <hi type="italic">those that go down to Egypt for help;</hi> for men's relation to the church will not secure them from divine woes if they live in contempt of divine laws. Observe, <div eID="gen16153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16154" type="x-p"/> I. What the sin was that is here reproved, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. Idolizing the Egyptians, and making court to them, as if happy were the people that had the Egyptians for their friends and allies. They <hi type="italic">go down to Egypt for help</hi> in every exigence, as if the worshippers of false gods had a better interest in heaven and were more likely to have success of earth than the servants of the living and true God. That which invited them to Egypt was that the Egyptians had many chariots to accommodate them with, and horses and horsemen that were strong; and, if they could get a good body of forces thence into their service, they would think themselves able to deal with the king of Assyria and his numerous army. Their kings were forbidden to multiply horses and chariots, and were told of the folly of trusting to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>); but they think themselves wiser than their Bible. 2. Slighting the God of Israel: <hi type="italic">They look not to the Holy One of Israel,</hi> as if he were not worth taking notice of in this distress. They advise not with him, seek not his favour, nor are in any care to make him their friend. <div eID="gen16154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16155" type="x-p"/> II. The gross absurdity and folly of this sin. 1. They neglected one whom, if they would not hope in him, they had reason to fear. They do not seek the Lord, nor make their application to him, <hi type="italic">yet he also is wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.2">v. 2</reference>. They are solicitous to get the Egyptians into an alliance with them, because they have the reputation of a politic people; and is not God wise too? and would not infinite wisdom, engaged on their side, stand them in more stead than all the policies of Egypt? They are at the pains of going down to Egypt, a tedious journey, when they might have had better advice, and better help, by looking up to heaven, and would not. But, if they will not court God's wisdom to act for them, they shall find it act against them. He is wise, too wise for them to outwit, and he will bring evil upon those who thus affront him. He will not call back his words as men do (because they are fickle and foolish), but he <hi type="italic">will arise against the house of the evil-doers,</hi> this cabal of them that go down to Egypt; God will appear to their confusion, according to the word that he has spoken, and will oppose the help they think to bring in from the workers of iniquity. Some think the Egyptians made it one condition of their coming into an alliance with him that they should worship the gods of Egypt, and they consented to it, and therefore they are both called <hi type="italic">evil-doers</hi> and <hi type="italic">workers of iniquity.</hi> 2. They trusted to those who were unable to help them and would soon appear to be so, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">v. 3</reference>. Let them know that <hi type="italic">the Egyptians,</hi> whom they depend so much upon, <hi type="italic">are men and not God.</hi> As it is good for men to <hi type="italic">know themselves to be but men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Ps. ix. 20</reference>), so it is good for us to consider that those we love and trust to are but men. They therefore can do nothing without God, nothing against him, nothing in comparison with him. They are men, and therefore fickle and foolish, mutable and mortal, here to day and gone to morrow; they are men, and therefore let us not make gods of them, by making them our hope and confidence, and expecting that in them which is to be found in God only; they are not God, they cannot do that for us which God can do, and will, if we trust in him. Let us not then neglect him, to seek to them; let us not forsake the rock of ages for broken reeds, nor the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. The Egyptians indeed have horses that are very strong; but <hi type="italic">they are flesh, and not spirit,</hi> and therefore, strong as they are, they may be wearied with a long march, and become unserviceable, or be wounded and slain in battle, and leave their riders to be ridden over. Every one knows this, that the Egyptians are not God and their horses are not spirit; but those that seek to them for help do not consider it, else they would not put such confidence in them. Sinners may be convicted of folly by the plainest and most self-evident truths, which they cannot deny, but will not believe. 3. They would certainly be ruined with the Egyptians they trusted in, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">When the Lord</hi> does but <hi type="italic">stretch out his hand</hi> how easily, how effectually, will he make them ashamed of their confidence in Egypt, and the Egyptians ashamed of the encouragement they gave them to trust in them; for <hi type="italic">he that helps and he that is helped shall fall together,</hi> and their mutual alliance shall prove their joint ruin. The Egyptians were shortly to be reckoned with, as appears by the <hi type="italic">burden of Egypt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.25">ch. xix.</reference>), and then those who fled to them for shelter and succour should fall with them; for there is no escaping the judgments of God. <hi type="italic">Evil pursues sinners,</hi> and it is just with God to make that creature a scourge to us which we make an idol of. 4. They took God's work out of his hands. They pretended a great deal of care to preserve Jerusalem, in advising to an alliance with Egypt; and, when others would not fall in with their measures, they pleaded self preservation, and went to Egypt themselves. Now the prophet here tells them that Jerusalem should be preserved without aid from Egypt and that those who tarried there should be safe when those who fled to Egypt should be ruined. Jerusalem was under God's protection, and therefore there was no occasion to put it under the protection of Egypt. But a practical distrust of God's all-sufficiency is at the bottom of all our sinful departures from him to the creature. The prophet tells them he had it from God's own mouth: <hi type="italic">Thus hath the Lord spoken to me.</hi> They might depend upon it, (1.) That God would appear against Jerusalem's enemies with the boldness of a <hi type="italic">lion over his prey,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">v. 4</reference>. When the lion comes out to seize his prey <hi type="italic">a multitude of shepherds come out against him;</hi> for it becomes neighbours to help one another when persons or goods are in danger. These shepherds dare not come near the lion; all they can do is to make a <hi type="italic">noise,</hi> and with that they think to frighten him off. But does he regard it? <hi type="italic">No: he will not be afraid of their voice,</hi> nor abase himself so far as to be in the least moved by it either to quit his prey or to make any more haste than otherwise he would do in seizing it. <hi type="italic">Thus will the Lord of hosts come down to fight for Mount Zion,</hi> with such an unshaken undaunted resolution not to be moved by any opposition; and he will as easily and irresistibly destroy the Assyrian army as a lion tears a lamb in pieces. Whoever appear against God, they are but like a multitude of poor simple shepherds shouting at a lion, who scorns to take notice of them or so much as to alter his pace for them. Surely those that have such a protector need not go to Egypt for help. (2.) That God would appear for Jerusalem's friends with the tenderness of a bird over her young, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.5">v. 5</reference>. God was ready to <hi type="italic">gather Jerusalem, as a hen gathers her brood under her wings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>); but those that trusted to the Egyptians would not be gathered. <hi type="italic">As birds flying</hi> to their nests with all possible speed, when they see them attacked, and fluttering about their nests with all possible concern, hovering over their young ones to protect them and drive away the assailants, with such compassion and affection <hi type="italic">will the Lord of hosts defend Jerusalem.</hi> As an eagle stirs up her young when they are in danger, <hi type="italic">takes them and bears them on her wings,</hi> so the Lord led Israel out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.11-Deut.32.12">Deut. xxxii. 11, 12</reference>); and he has now the same tender concern for them that he had then, so that they need not flee into Egypt again for shelter. <hi type="italic">Defending, he will deliver it;</hi> he will so defend it as to secure the continuance of its safety, not defend it for a while and abandon it at last, but defend it so that it shall not fall into the enemies' hand. <hi type="italic">I will defend this city to save it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.37.35">ch. xxxvii. 35</reference>. <hi type="italic">Passing over he will preserve it;</hi> the word for passing over is used in this sense only here and <reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Exod. xii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.23">23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.27">27</reference>, concerning the destroying angel's passing over the houses of the Israelites when he slew all the first-born of the Egyptians, to which story this passage refers. The Assyrian army was to be routed by a destroying angel, who should pass over Jerusalem, though that deserved to be destroyed, and draw his sword only against the besiegers. They shall be slain by the pestilence, but none of the besieged shall take the infection. Thus he will again pass over the houses of his people and secure them.

When the Lord shall stretch out his hand, both he that helpeth shall fall, and he that is holpen shall fall down, and they all shall fail together. 4 For thus hath the Lord spoken unto me, Like as the lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, when a multitude of shepherds is called forth against him, he will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them: so shall the Lord of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion, and for the hill thereof. 5 As birds flying, so will the Lord of hosts defend Jerusalem; defending also he will deliver it; and passing over he will preserve it. Observe, I. What the sin was that is here reproved, v. 1 . 1. Idolizing the Egyptians, and making court to them, as if happy were the people that had the Egyptians for their friends and allies. They go down to Egypt for help in every exigence, as if the worshippers of false gods had a better interest in heaven and were more likely to have success of earth than the servants of the living and true God. That which invited them to Egypt was that the Egyptians had many chariots to accommodate them with, and horses and horsemen that were strong; and, if they could get a good body of forces thence into their service, they would think themselves able to deal with the king of Assyria and his numerous army. Their kings were forbidden to multiply horses and chariots, and were told of the folly of trusting to them ( Ps. xx. 7 ); but they think themselves wiser than their Bible. 2. Slighting the God of Israel: They look not to the Holy One of Israel, as if he were not worth taking notice of in this distress. They advise not with him, seek not his favour, nor are in any care to make him their friend. II. The gross absurdity and folly of this sin. 1. They neglected one whom, if they would not hope in him, they had reason to fear. They do not seek the Lord, nor make their application to him, yet he also is wise, v. 2 . They are at the pains of going down to Egypt, a tedious journey, when they might have had better advice, and better help, by looking up to heaven, and would not. But, if they will not court God's wisdom to act for them, they shall find it act against them. He is wise, too wise for them to outwit, and he will bring evil upon those who thus affront him. He will not call back his words as men do (because they are fickle and foolish), but he will arise against the house of the evil-doers, this cabal of them that go down to Egypt; God will appear to their confusion, according to the word that he has spoken, and will oppose the help they think to bring in from the workers of iniquity. Some think the Egyptians made it one condition of their coming into an alliance with him that they should worship the gods of Egypt, and they consented to it, and therefore they are both called evil-doers and workers of iniquity. 2. They trusted to those who were unable to help them and would soon appear to be so, v. 3 . Let them know that the Egyptians, whom they depend so much upon, are men and not God. As it is good for men to know themselves to be but men ( Ps. ix. 20 ), so it is good for us to consider that those we love and trust to are but men. They therefore can do nothing without God, nothing against him, nothing in comparison with him. They are men, and therefore fickle and foolish, mutable and mortal, here to day and gone to morrow; they are men, and therefore let us not make gods of them, by making them our hope and confidence, and expecting that in them which is to be found in God only; they are not God, they cannot do that for us which God can do, and will, if we trust in him. Let us not then neglect him, to seek to them; let us not forsake the rock of ages for broken reeds, nor the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. I will defend this city to save it, ch. xxxvii. 35 . Passing over he will preserve it; the word for passing over is used in this sense only here and Exod. xii. 12 , 23 , 27 , concerning the destroying angel's passing over the houses of the Israelites when he slew all the first-born of the Egyptians, to which story this passage refers. The Assyrian army was to be routed by a destroying angel, who should pass over Jerusalem, though that deserved to be destroyed, and draw his sword only against the besiegers. As an eagle stirs up her young when they are in danger, takes them and bears them on her wings, so the Lord led Israel out of Egypt ( Deut. xxxii. 11, 12 ); and he has now the same tender concern for them that he had then, so that they need not flee into Egypt again for shelter. Defending, he will deliver it; he will so defend it as to secure the continuance of its safety, not defend it for a while and abandon it at last, but defend it so that it shall not fall into the enemies' hand. I will defend this city to save it, ch. xxxvii. 35 . Passing over he will preserve it; the word for passing over is used in this sense only here and Exod. xii. 12 , 23 , 27 , concerning the destroying angel's passing over the houses of the Israelites when he slew all the first-born of the Egyptians, to which story this passage refers. The Assyrian army was to be routed by a destroying angel, who should pass over Jerusalem, though that deserved to be destroyed, and draw his sword only against the besiegers. They shall be slain by the pestilence, but none of the besieged shall take the infection. Thus he will again pass over the houses of his people and secure them.
entries.reader_content_osis: <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because <hi type="italic">they are</hi> many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ! <hi type="super">2</hi> Yet he also <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise, and will bring evil, and will not call back his words: but will arise against the house of the evildoers, and against the help of them that work iniquity. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now the Egyptians <hi type="italic">are</hi> men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall stretch out his hand, both he that helpeth shall fall, and he that is holpen shall fall down, and they all shall fail together. <hi type="super">4</hi> For thus hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spoken unto me, Like as the lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, when a multitude of shepherds is called forth against him, <hi type="italic">he</hi> will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them: so shall the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion, and for the hill thereof. <hi type="super">5</hi> As birds flying, so will the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts defend Jerusalem; defending also he will deliver <hi type="italic">it; and</hi> passing over he will preserve it. <div eID="gen16152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16153" type="x-p"/> This is the last of four chapters together that begin with woe; and they are all woes to the sinners that were found among the professing people of God, to the <hi type="italic">drunkards of Ephraim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">ch. xxviii. 1</reference>), to <hi type="italic">Ariel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">ch. xxix. 1</reference>), to the <hi type="italic">rebellious children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.1">ch. xxx. 1</reference>), and here to <hi type="italic">those that go down to Egypt for help;</hi> for men's relation to the church will not secure them from divine woes if they live in contempt of divine laws. Observe, <div eID="gen16153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16154" type="x-p"/> I. What the sin was that is here reproved, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. Idolizing the Egyptians, and making court to them, as if happy were the people that had the Egyptians for their friends and allies. They <hi type="italic">go down to Egypt for help</hi> in every exigence, as if the worshippers of false gods had a better interest in heaven and were more likely to have success of earth than the servants of the living and true God. That which invited them to Egypt was that the Egyptians had many chariots to accommodate them with, and horses and horsemen that were strong; and, if they could get a good body of forces thence into their service, they would think themselves able to deal with the king of Assyria and his numerous army. Their kings were forbidden to multiply horses and chariots, and were told of the folly of trusting to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>); but they think themselves wiser than their Bible. 2. Slighting the God of Israel: <hi type="italic">They look not to the Holy One of Israel,</hi> as if he were not worth taking notice of in this distress. They advise not with him, seek not his favour, nor are in any care to make him their friend. <div eID="gen16154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16155" type="x-p"/> II. The gross absurdity and folly of this sin. 1. They neglected one whom, if they would not hope in him, they had reason to fear. They do not seek the Lord, nor make their application to him, <hi type="italic">yet he also is wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.2">v. 2</reference>. They are solicitous to get the Egyptians into an alliance with them, because they have the reputation of a politic people; and is not God wise too? and would not infinite wisdom, engaged on their side, stand them in more stead than all the policies of Egypt? They are at the pains of going down to Egypt, a tedious journey, when they might have had better advice, and better help, by looking up to heaven, and would not. But, if they will not court God's wisdom to act for them, they shall find it act against them. He is wise, too wise for them to outwit, and he will bring evil upon those who thus affront him. He will not call back his words as men do (because they are fickle and foolish), but he <hi type="italic">will arise against the house of the evil-doers,</hi> this cabal of them that go down to Egypt; God will appear to their confusion, according to the word that he has spoken, and will oppose the help they think to bring in from the workers of iniquity. Some think the Egyptians made it one condition of their coming into an alliance with him that they should worship the gods of Egypt, and they consented to it, and therefore they are both called <hi type="italic">evil-doers</hi> and <hi type="italic">workers of iniquity.</hi> 2. They trusted to those who were unable to help them and would soon appear to be so, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">v. 3</reference>. Let them know that <hi type="italic">the Egyptians,</hi> whom they depend so much upon, <hi type="italic">are men and not God.</hi> As it is good for men to <hi type="italic">know themselves to be but men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Ps. ix. 20</reference>), so it is good for us to consider that those we love and trust to are but men. They therefore can do nothing without God, nothing against him, nothing in comparison with him. They are men, and therefore fickle and foolish, mutable and mortal, here to day and gone to morrow; they are men, and therefore let us not make gods of them, by making them our hope and confidence, and expecting that in them which is to be found in God only; they are not God, they cannot do that for us which God can do, and will, if we trust in him. Let us not then neglect him, to seek to them; let us not forsake the rock of ages for broken reeds, nor the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. The Egyptians indeed have horses that are very strong; but <hi type="italic">they are flesh, and not spirit,</hi> and therefore, strong as they are, they may be wearied with a long march, and become unserviceable, or be wounded and slain in battle, and leave their riders to be ridden over. Every one knows this, that the Egyptians are not God and their horses are not spirit; but those that seek to them for help do not consider it, else they would not put such confidence in them. Sinners may be convicted of folly by the plainest and most self-evident truths, which they cannot deny, but will not believe. 3. They would certainly be ruined with the Egyptians they trusted in, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">When the Lord</hi> does but <hi type="italic">stretch out his hand</hi> how easily, how effectually, will he make them ashamed of their confidence in Egypt, and the Egyptians ashamed of the encouragement they gave them to trust in them; for <hi type="italic">he that helps and he that is helped shall fall together,</hi> and their mutual alliance shall prove their joint ruin. The Egyptians were shortly to be reckoned with, as appears by the <hi type="italic">burden of Egypt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.25">ch. xix.</reference>), and then those who fled to them for shelter and succour should fall with them; for there is no escaping the judgments of God. <hi type="italic">Evil pursues sinners,</hi> and it is just with God to make that creature a scourge to us which we make an idol of. 4. They took God's work out of his hands. They pretended a great deal of care to preserve Jerusalem, in advising to an alliance with Egypt; and, when others would not fall in with their measures, they pleaded self preservation, and went to Egypt themselves. Now the prophet here tells them that Jerusalem should be preserved without aid from Egypt and that those who tarried there should be safe when those who fled to Egypt should be ruined. Jerusalem was under God's protection, and therefore there was no occasion to put it under the protection of Egypt. But a practical distrust of God's all-sufficiency is at the bottom of all our sinful departures from him to the creature. The prophet tells them he had it from God's own mouth: <hi type="italic">Thus hath the Lord spoken to me.</hi> They might depend upon it, (1.) That God would appear against Jerusalem's enemies with the boldness of a <hi type="italic">lion over his prey,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">v. 4</reference>. When the lion comes out to seize his prey <hi type="italic">a multitude of shepherds come out against him;</hi> for it becomes neighbours to help one another when persons or goods are in danger. These shepherds dare not come near the lion; all they can do is to make a <hi type="italic">noise,</hi> and with that they think to frighten him off. But does he regard it? <hi type="italic">No: he will not be afraid of their voice,</hi> nor abase himself so far as to be in the least moved by it either to quit his prey or to make any more haste than otherwise he would do in seizing it. <hi type="italic">Thus will the Lord of hosts come down to fight for Mount Zion,</hi> with such an unshaken undaunted resolution not to be moved by any opposition; and he will as easily and irresistibly destroy the Assyrian army as a lion tears a lamb in pieces. Whoever appear against God, they are but like a multitude of poor simple shepherds shouting at a lion, who scorns to take notice of them or so much as to alter his pace for them. Surely those that have such a protector need not go to Egypt for help. (2.) That God would appear for Jerusalem's friends with the tenderness of a bird over her young, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.5">v. 5</reference>. God was ready to <hi type="italic">gather Jerusalem, as a hen gathers her brood under her wings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>); but those that trusted to the Egyptians would not be gathered. <hi type="italic">As birds flying</hi> to their nests with all possible speed, when they see them attacked, and fluttering about their nests with all possible concern, hovering over their young ones to protect them and drive away the assailants, with such compassion and affection <hi type="italic">will the Lord of hosts defend Jerusalem.</hi> As an eagle stirs up her young when they are in danger, <hi type="italic">takes them and bears them on her wings,</hi> so the Lord led Israel out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.11-Deut.32.12">Deut. xxxii. 11, 12</reference>); and he has now the same tender concern for them that he had then, so that they need not flee into Egypt again for shelter. <hi type="italic">Defending, he will deliver it;</hi> he will so defend it as to secure the continuance of its safety, not defend it for a while and abandon it at last, but defend it so that it shall not fall into the enemies' hand. <hi type="italic">I will defend this city to save it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.37.35">ch. xxxvii. 35</reference>. <hi type="italic">Passing over he will preserve it;</hi> the word for passing over is used in this sense only here and <reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Exod. xii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.23">23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.27">27</reference>, concerning the destroying angel's passing over the houses of the Israelites when he slew all the first-born of the Egyptians, to which story this passage refers. The Assyrian army was to be routed by a destroying angel, who should pass over Jerusalem, though that deserved to be destroyed, and draw his sword only against the besiegers. They shall be slain by the pestilence, but none of the besieged shall take the infection. Thus he will again pass over the houses of his people and secure them.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen16155" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Call to Repentance; Deliverance of Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen16156" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Turn ye unto <hi type="italic">him from</hi> whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted. <hi type="super">7</hi> For in that day every man shall cast away his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which your own hands have made unto you <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sin. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then shall the Assyrian fall with the sword, not of a mighty man; and the sword, not of a mean man, shall devour him: but he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be discomfited. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he shall pass over to his strong hold for fear, and his princes shall be afraid of the ensign, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , whose fire <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem. <div eID="gen16156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16157" type="x-p"/> This explains the foregoing promise of the deliverance of Jerusalem; she shall be fitted for deliverance, and then it shall be wrought for her; for in that method God delivers. <div eID="gen16157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16158" type="x-p"/> I. Jerusalem shall be reformed, and so she shall be delivered from her enemies within her walls, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.6-Isa.31.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Here is, 1. A gracious call to repentance. This was the Lord's voice crying in the city, the voice of the rod, the voice of the sword, and the voice of the prophets interpreting the judgment: "<hi type="italic">Turn you,</hi> O turn you now, from your evil ways, <hi type="italic">unto God,</hi> return to your allegiance to him <hi type="italic">from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted,</hi> from whom you, <hi type="italic">O children of Israel!</hi> have revolted." He reminds them of their birth and parentage, that they were <hi type="italic">children of Israel,</hi> and therefore under the highest obligations imaginable to the God of Israel, as an aggravation of their revolt from him and as an encouragement to them to return to him. "They have been backsliding children, yet children; therefore let them return, and their backslidings shall be healed. They have deeply revolted, with great address as they supposed (<hi type="italic">the revolters are profound,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.5.2">Hos. v. 2</reference>); but the issue will prove that they have revolted dangerously. The stain of their sins has gone deeply into their nature, not to be easily got out, like the blackness of the Ethiopian. <hi type="italic">They have deeply corrupted themselves</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.9">Hos. ix. 9</reference>); they have sunk deep into misery, and cannot easily recover themselves; therefore you have need to hasten your return to God." 2. A gracious promise of the good success of this call (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">In that day every man shall cast away his idols,</hi> in obedience to Hezekiah's orders, which, till they were alarmed by the Assyrian invasion, many refused to do. That is a happy fright which frightens us from our sins. (1.) It shall be a general reformation: every man shall cast away his own idols, shall begin with them before he undertakes to demolish other people's idols, which there will be no need of when every man reforms himself. (2.) It shall be a thorough reformation; for they shall part with their idolatry, their beloved sin, with their <hi type="italic">idols of silver and gold,</hi> their idols that they are most fond of. Many make an idol of their silver and gold, and by the love of that idol are drawn to revolt from God; but those that turn to God cast that away out of their hearts and will be ready to part with it when God calls. (3.) It shall be a reformation upon a right principle, a principle of piety, not of politics. They shall cast away their idols, because they have been unto them <hi type="italic">for a sin,</hi> an occasion of sin; therefore they will have nothing to do with them, though they had been the work of their <hi type="italic">own hands,</hi> and upon that account they had a particular fondness for them. Sin is the work of our own hands, but in working it we have been working our own ruin, and therefore we must cast it away; and those are strangely wedded to it who will not be prevailed upon to cast it away when they see that otherwise they themselves will be castaways. Some make this to be only a prediction that those who trust in idols, when they find they stand them in no stead, will cast them away in indignation. But it agrees so exactly with <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">ch. xxx. 22</reference> that I rather take it as a promise of a sincere reformation. <div eID="gen16158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16159" type="x-p"/> II. Jerusalem's besiegers shall be routed, and so she shall be delivered from the enemies about her walls. The former makes way for this. If a people return to God, they may leave it to him to plead their cause against their enemies. When they have cast away their idols, <hi type="italic">then shall the Assyrian fall,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8-Isa.31.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. 1. The army of the Assyrians shall be laid dead upon the spot <hi type="italic">by the sword, not of a mighty man, nor of a mean man,</hi> not of any man at all, either Israelite or Egyptian, not forcibly by the sword of a mighty man nor surreptitiously by the sword of a mean man, but by the sword of an angel, who strikes more strongly than a mighty man and yet more secretly than a mean man, by the sword of the Lord, and his power and wrath in the hand of the angel. Thus the young men of the army shall melt, and be discomfited, and become tributaries to death. When God has work to do against the enemies of his church we expect it must be done by mighty men and mean men, officers and common soldiers; whereas God can, if he please, do it without either. <hi type="italic">He</hi> needs not armies of men who has legions of angels at command, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.53">Matt. xxvi. 53</reference>. 2. The king of Assyria shall flee for the same, shall flee from that invisible sword, hoping to get out of the reach of it; and he shall make the best of his way to his own dominions, shall pass over to some strong-hold of his own, for fear lest the Jews should pursue him now that his army was routed. Sennacherib had been very confident that he should make himself master of Jerusalem, and in the most insolent manner had set both God and Hezekiah at defiance; yet now he is made to tremble for fear of both. God can strike a terror into the proudest of men, and make the stoutest heart to tremble. See <reference osisRef="Job.18.11">Job xviii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.24">xx. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">His princes</hi> that accompany him <hi type="italic">shall be afraid of the ensign,</hi> shall be in a continual fright at the remembrance of the ensign in the air, which perhaps the destroying angel displayed before he gave the fatal bow. Or they shall be afraid of every ensign they see, suspecting it is a party of the Jews pursuing them. The banner that God displays for the encouragement of his people (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.4">Ps. lx. 4</reference>) will be a terror to his and their enemies. Thus he <hi type="italic">cuts off the spirit of princes and is terrible to the kings of the earth.</hi> But who will do this? It is <hi type="italic">the Lord, whose fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem.</hi> (1.) Whose residence is there, and who there keeps house, as a man does where his fire and his oven are. It is the city of the great King, and let not the Assyrians think to turn him out of the possession of his own house. (2.) Who is there a consuming fire to all his enemies and will make them as a fiery oven in the day of his wrath, <reference osisRef="Ps.21.9">Ps. xxi. 9</reference>. He is himself <hi type="italic">a wall of fire round about Jerusalem,</hi> so that whoever assaults her does so at his peril, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zech. ii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.5">Rev. xi. 5</reference>. (3.) Who has his altar there, on which the holy fire is continually kept burning and sacrifices are daily offered to his honour, and with which he is well pleased; and therefore he will defend this city, especially having an eye to the great sacrifice which was there also to be offered, of which all the sacrifices were types. If we keep up the fire of holy love and devotion in our hearts and houses, we may depend upon God to be a protection to us and them.  <chapter eID="Isa.31"/> <div eID="gen16159" type="x-p"/>

( b. c. 720.) 6 Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted. 7 For in that day every man shall cast away his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which your own hands have made unto you for a sin. 8 Then shall the Assyrian fall with the sword, not of a mighty man; and the sword, not of a mean man, shall devour him: but he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be discomfited. 9 And he shall pass over to his strong hold for fear, and his princes shall be afraid of the ensign, saith the Lord , whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem. This explains the foregoing promise of the deliverance of Jerusalem; she shall be fitted for deliverance, and then it shall be wrought for her; for in that method God delivers. I. He reminds them of their birth and parentage, that they were children of Israel, and therefore under the highest obligations imaginable to the God of Israel, as an aggravation of their revolt from him and as an encouragement to them to return to him. They have deeply corrupted themselves ( Hos. ix. 9 ); they have sunk deep into misery, and cannot easily recover themselves; therefore you have need to hasten your return to God." 2. But it agrees so exactly with ch. xxx. 22 that I rather take it as a promise of a sincere reformation. II. Jerusalem's besiegers shall be routed, and so she shall be delivered from the enemies about her walls. The former makes way for this. If a people return to God, they may leave it to him to plead their cause against their enemies. When they have cast away their idols, then shall the Assyrian fall, v. 8, 9 . 1. The army of the Assyrians shall be laid dead upon the spot by the sword, not of a mighty man, nor of a mean man, not of any man at all, either Israelite or Egyptian, not forcibly by the sword of a mighty man nor surreptitiously by the sword of a mean man, but by the sword of an angel, who strikes more strongly than a mighty man and yet more secretly than a mean man, by the sword of the Lord, and his power and wrath in the hand of the angel. Thus the young men of the army shall melt, and be discomfited, and become tributaries to death. When God has work to do against the enemies of his church we expect it must be done by mighty men and mean men, officers and common soldiers; whereas God can, if he please, do it without either. He needs not armies of men who has legions of angels at command, Matt. xxvi. 53 . 2. The king of Assyria shall flee for the same, shall flee from that invisible sword, hoping to get out of the reach of it; and he shall make the best of his way to his own dominions, shall pass over to some strong-hold of his own, for fear lest the Jews should pursue him now that his army was routed. Or they shall be afraid of every ensign they see, suspecting it is a party of the Jews pursuing them. The banner that God displays for the encouragement of his people ( Ps. lx. 4 ) will be a terror to his and their enemies. Thus he cuts off the spirit of princes and is terrible to the kings of the earth. But who will do this? It is the Lord, whose fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem. (1.) Whose residence is there, and who there keeps house, as a man does where his fire and his oven are. It is the city of the great King, and let not the Assyrians think to turn him out of the possession of his own house. (2.) Who is there a consuming fire to all his enemies and will make them as a fiery oven in the day of his wrath, Ps. xxi. 9 . He is himself a wall of fire round about Jerusalem, so that whoever assaults her does so at his peril, Zech. ii. 5 ; Rev. xi. 5 . (3.) Jerusalem shall be reformed, and so she shall be delivered from her enemies within her walls, v. 6, 7 . Here is, 1. A gracious call to repentance. This was the Lord's voice crying in the city, the voice of the rod, the voice of the sword, and the voice of the prophets interpreting the judgment: " Turn you, O turn you now, from your evil ways, unto God, return to your allegiance to him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted, from whom you, O children of Israel! have revolted." He reminds them of their birth and parentage, that they were children of Israel, and therefore under the highest obligations imaginable to the God of Israel, as an aggravation of their revolt from him and as an encouragement to them to return to him. "They have been backsliding children, yet children; therefore let them return, and their backslidings shall be healed. They have deeply revolted, with great address as they supposed ( the revolters are profound, Hos. v. 2 ); but the issue will prove that they have revolted dangerously. The stain of their sins has gone deeply into their nature, not to be easily got out, like the blackness of the Ethiopian. They have deeply corrupted themselves ( Hos. ix. 9 ); they have sunk deep into misery, and cannot easily recover themselves; therefore you have need to hasten your return to God." 2. A gracious promise of the good success of this call ( v. 7 ): In that day every man shall cast away his idols, in obedience to Hezekiah's orders, which, till they were alarmed by the Assyrian invasion, many refused to do. That is a happy fright which frightens us from our sins. (1.) It shall be a general reformation: every man shall cast away his own idols, shall begin with them before he undertakes to demolish other people's idols, which there will be no need of when every man reforms himself. (2.) It shall be a thorough reformation; for they shall part with their idolatry, their beloved sin, with their idols of silver and gold, their idols that they are most fond of. Many make an idol of their silver and gold, and by the love of that idol are drawn to revolt from God; but those that turn to God cast that away out of their hearts and will be ready to part with it when God calls. (3.) It shall be a reformation upon a right principle, a principle of piety, not of politics. They shall cast away their idols, because they have been unto them for a sin, an occasion of sin; therefore they will have nothing to do with them, though they had been the work of their own hands, and upon that account they had a particular fondness for them. Sin is the work of our own hands, but in working it we have been working our own ruin, and therefore we must cast it away; and those are strangely wedded to it who will not be prevailed upon to cast it away when they see that otherwise they themselves will be castaways. Some make this to be only a prediction that those who trust in idols, when they find they stand them in no stead, will cast them away in indignation. But it agrees so exactly with ch. xxx. 22 that I rather take it as a promise of a sincere reformation. II. Jerusalem's besiegers shall be routed, and so she shall be delivered from the enemies about her walls. The former makes way for this. If a people return to God, they may leave it to him to plead their cause against their enemies. When they have cast away their idols, then shall the Assyrian fall, v. 8, 9 . 1. The army of the Assyrians shall be laid dead upon the spot by the sword, not of a mighty man, nor of a mean man, not of any man at all, either Israelite or Egyptian, not forcibly by the sword of a mighty man nor surreptitiously by the sword of a mean man, but by the sword of an angel, who strikes more strongly than a mighty man and yet more secretly than a mean man, by the sword of the Lord, and his power and wrath in the hand of the angel. Thus the young men of the army shall melt, and be discomfited, and become tributaries to death. When God has work to do against the enemies of his church we expect it must be done by mighty men and mean men, officers and common soldiers; whereas God can, if he please, do it without either. He needs not armies of men who has legions of angels at command, Matt. xxvi. 53 . 2. The king of Assyria shall flee for the same, shall flee from that invisible sword, hoping to get out of the reach of it; and he shall make the best of his way to his own dominions, shall pass over to some strong-hold of his own, for fear lest the Jews should pursue him now that his army was routed. Sennacherib had been very confident that he should make himself master of Jerusalem, and in the most insolent manner had set both God and Hezekiah at defiance; yet now he is made to tremble for fear of both. God can strike a terror into the proudest of men, and make the stoutest heart to tremble. See Job xviii. 11 ; xx. 24 . His princes that accompany him shall be afraid of the ensign, shall be in a continual fright at the remembrance of the ensign in the air, which perhaps the destroying angel displayed before he gave the fatal bow. Or they shall be afraid of every ensign they see, suspecting it is a party of the Jews pursuing them. The banner that God displays for the encouragement of his people ( Ps. lx. 4 ) will be a terror to his and their enemies. Thus he cuts off the spirit of princes and is terrible to the kings of the earth. But who will do this? It is the Lord, whose fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem. (1.) Whose residence is there, and who there keeps house, as a man does where his fire and his oven are. It is the city of the great King, and let not the Assyrians think to turn him out of the possession of his own house. (2.) Who is there a consuming fire to all his enemies and will make them as a fiery oven in the day of his wrath, Ps. xxi. 9 . He is himself a wall of fire round about Jerusalem, so that whoever assaults her does so at his peril, Zech. ii. 5 ; Rev. xi. 5 . (3.) Who has his altar there, on which the holy fire is continually kept burning and sacrifices are daily offered to his honour, and with which he is well pleased; and therefore he will defend this city, especially having an eye to the great sacrifice which was there also to be offered, of which all the sacrifices were types. If we keep up the fire of holy love and devotion in our hearts and houses, we may depend upon God to be a protection to us and them.

A woe to those who, when the Assyrian army invaded them, trusted to the Egyptians, and not to God, for succour, ver. 1-3 . II. Assurance given of the care God would take of Jerusalem in that time of danger and distress, ver. 4, 5 . III. A call to repentance and reformation, ver. 6, 7 . IV. A prediction of the fall of the Assyrian army, and the fright which the Assyrian king should thereby be put into, ver. 8, 9 .
